scenarios.context: Your ads ranking team trains models offline on historical logs but serves them online at 50k QPS with a p99 latency budget of 20ms. Today, training and serving compute features with two different code paths, and nobody is sure they match.
scenarios.goal: Design a feature store that guarantees training/serving consistency at scale.

questions.question: How do features get from raw events into the store, and how do you guarantee the training data matches what serving saw?
questions.strong: Log feature values with event timestamps into an immutable offline log; serving reads use as-of lookups; training joins labels to the feature values as they were at event time, never current values.
questions.why: Point-in-time correctness is the core hard problem of feature stores.

questions.question: Online store vs offline store: what lives where, and why two stores?
questions.strong: Online: low-latency key-value store with TTLs for point lookups; offline: columnar store for full scans and training joins; materialization jobs keep them in sync.

questions.question: A feature pipeline breaks for 3 hours and then recovers. How do you backfill without corrupting training data?
questions.strong: Recompute from raw events using event time, not processing time; version the backfilled range; never let backfilled values leak future information into past rows.

questions.question: Some features are expensive aggregates (e.g. 30-day purchase counts per user). How do you balance freshness against compute cost?
questions.strong: Tier features: streaming for the critical few, batch for the rest; TTLs matched to staleness tolerance; approximate aggregates where exactness does not move the metric.

questions.question: How do teams discover, version, and deprecate features?
questions.strong: A feature registry with ownership, schemas, and lineage; versioned definitions; a deprecation policy so zombie features do not accumulate forever.
questions.why: The organizational side: a store is a platform.

questions.question: What do you monitor for the feature store itself?
questions.strong: Freshness SLAs, null and default rates, distribution drift per feature, and online/offline parity checks that page when training and serving diverge.
questions.why: Monitoring the platform, not just the model.

rubric.check: Trace raw events through ingestion, materialization, and online/offline stores.
Name concrete features, tiers, TTLs, and backfill/versioning discipline.
Guarantee point-in-time correctness; check online/offline parity.
Meet p99 20ms: KV lookups, precomputation, and fallback paths.
Freshness SLAs, null rates, drift, and parity checks with paging.
Name how serving decisions feed back into training data (selection bias).

scenarios.title: Feature Store for Real-Time Ranking

scenarios.context: Your churn model retrains weekly on fresh data. Last month a bad retrain shipped silently and emailed 10k wrong 'at-risk' flags to the sales team before anyone noticed.
scenarios.goal: Design a safe, reproducible batch retraining pipeline.

questions.question: Walk me through the pipeline stages from raw data to a promoted model.
questions.strong: Ingest, validate, train, evaluate against gates, then promote; each stage is a discrete, logged, retryable step, not a notebook.

questions.question: How do you validate the data before training starts?
questions.strong: Schema checks, null and range checks, distribution checks against a baseline; fail the run loudly instead of training on garbage.

questions.question: When does the new model replace the old one, and when does it NOT?
questions.strong: Champion/challenger with metric gates on backtest and calibration; auto-promote small wins, require human approval for big behavior changes; never promote on training metrics.

questions.question: The new model is worse in production. How do you roll back, and how fast?
questions.strong: Versioned model artifacts with one-click rollback to the previous champion; rollback tested in game days; minutes, not hours.

questions.question: How do you guarantee reproducibility of any past training run?
questions.strong: Snapshot the training data, version code plus config plus dependencies, log full lineage from raw tables to artifact.

questions.question: What alerts fire at 3am, and what can wait until morning?
questions.strong: Page on: pipeline failure blocking promotion, validation failures on critical features, rollback events; ticket on: minor metric wiggles, slow steps.

rubric.check: Stage the pipeline: ingest, validate, train, evaluate, promote, with logging.
Validate schema, nulls, ranges, and distributions before training.
Promotion gates, champion/challenger, calibration checks; never promote on train metrics.
Bounded pipeline runtime; rollback in minutes; SLA on retrain cadence.
Tiered alerts: page on failures and bad promotions, ticket on wiggles.
Track how the deployed model's actions change the data the next retrain sees.

scenarios.title: Batch Retraining Pipeline

scenarios.context: Your fraud model scores 10k transactions per second with a p99 budget of 100ms. A bad deploy blocks legitimate payments, which is a revenue incident, so you cannot just ship and hope.
scenarios.goal: Design model serving with shadow deployment and safe rollout.

questions.question: How does a request flow through serving, and where does the model live?
questions.strong: Feature fetch, then inference: either a dedicated model server or an embedded runtime; separate the concerns of feature retrieval and scoring.

questions.question: What exactly is shadow mode, and what do you compare between shadow and live?
questions.strong: Duplicate live traffic to the new model without affecting responses; log its predictions; compare score distributions, agreement rate, latency, and estimated business metrics.

questions.question: How do you graduate from shadow to canary to full rollout?
questions.strong: Shadow, then 1% canary, then ramp on fixed success criteria; automatic halt and rollback if guardrails breach; each stage has a bake time.

questions.question: What is your kill switch, and how fast does it work?
questions.strong: A config flag or traffic router that reverts to the previous version instantly; tested regularly in game days, not invented during the incident.

questions.question: How do you version models and keep backward compatibility?
questions.strong: A model registry with immutable versions; schema-versioned inputs/outputs; canary by version so two versions can serve side by side.

questions.question: What do you monitor during the rollout?
questions.strong: Latency, error rate, prediction distribution shift, business metrics (approval rate, fraud loss); compare shadow vs live continuously, not just at launch.

rubric.check: Request path: feature fetch, inference, logging; where the model lives.
Feature retrieval separated from scoring; versioned feature schemas.
Shadow comparison of distributions and agreement before any live traffic.
p99 100ms budget: where time goes, timeouts, and fallback behavior.
Latency, errors, prediction drift, business metrics; kill switch tested.
Log shadow predictions for future training; watch decisions reshaping data.

scenarios.title: Model Serving with Shadow Deploy

scenarios.context: Fifty teams run A/B tests on your platform. Last quarter two launches were called on noisy metrics, and one 'winner' turned out to be a tracking bug, not a product win.

questions.question: How do you assign users to variants, and why does the unit of randomization matter?
questions.strong: Hash-based sticky assignment; the unit (user, session, cluster) must match the treatment's scope; cluster randomization when there is interference.

questions.question: An experiment shows a win on day 2. Why should you not ship it?
questions.strong: Peeking inflates false positives; runtime and success criteria are pre-registered; early wins often regress; novelty effects fade.

questions.question: How do you catch a broken experiment, and what other data-quality checks run?
questions.strong: Sample ratio mismatch (SRM) checks, pre-period A/A validation, guardrail metrics, and tracking-health checks that catch logging bugs before they become 'wins'.

questions.question: How do you reduce variance so teams can detect smaller effects faster?
questions.strong: CUPED with pre-period covariates, stratification, and right-sized runtimes; explain the trade-off between speed and the risk of short-term-only effects.

questions.question: How do you handle overlapping experiments and interference between them?
questions.strong: Mutual-exclusion layers or namespaces for conflicting tests; interaction analysis; cluster or geo randomization for network-effect features.

questions.question: What guardrails stop a bad experiment from hurting the business?
questions.strong: Automatic shutoff on guardrail breaches, required review for risky tests, and a launch checklist that includes metric health, not just the primary win.

rubric.check: Assignment service, logging, metric computation, and results surfacing.
Covariates for variance reduction; pre-period data plumbing.
SRM checks, A/A validation, and tracking health before trusting results.
Time-to-result: fast assignment, daily metric refreshes, runtime guidance.
Guardrail metrics, automatic shutoff, experiment health dashboards.
Novelty effects, interference between experiments, and winner's-curse follow-ups.

scenarios.title: Experimentation Platform

scenarios.context: An upstream schema change silently nulled a key model feature. The model degraded for two weeks before anyone noticed, because no check watched the data.
scenarios.goal: Design data quality monitoring for ML pipelines.

questions.question: What checks run on every batch or stream of data, and where do they live?
questions.strong: Schema, null rates, value ranges, and volume checks; run at ingestion and again right before training and serving, so bad data fails fast at the boundary.
questions.why: Breadth of the check suite and placement.

questions.question: How do you detect distribution drift versus a one-off anomaly?
questions.strong: PSI or KS tests against a baseline, with seasonality-aware thresholds; a one-off spike recovers, drift persists; different responses for each.

questions.question: How do you set alert thresholds that do not page people to death?
questions.strong: Severity tiers, anomaly detection on the metrics themselves, and tuned thresholds from historical data; every page must be actionable.
questions.why: Alert fatigue is the failure mode of monitoring.

questions.question: A critical feature goes stale. What is the automated response?
questions.strong: Fall back to default or last-known-good values, degrade to a simpler model, and block new promotions until freshness recovers; never silently serve stale features.

questions.question: How do you trace a bad prediction back to the data that caused it?
questions.strong: Full lineage from raw tables through features to predictions; logged feature values per prediction; data snapshots so any incident is replayable.

questions.question: How do you measure whether the monitoring itself is working?
questions.strong: Time-to-detect on past incidents, false-positive rate of alerts, and postmortems that ask why the check did not fire sooner.

rubric.check: Checks at ingestion and at the training/serving boundary; fail fast.
Schema, null, range, and volume checks per feature.
Detect drift with PSI/KS vs baseline; separate drift from one-off anomalies.
Time-to-detect; checks cheap enough to run on every batch.
Tiered, actionable alerts; automated fallback on stale features.
Lineage from raw data to prediction; meta-metrics on the monitoring itself.

scenarios.title: Data Quality Monitoring

scenarios.context: You are building semantic search over 100M documents for a RAG product. The requirement is p99 latency under 100ms with recall above 0.95 versus brute-force search.

questions.question: Walk me through the pipeline from a document to a searchable vector.
questions.strong: Chunking strategy, embedding model, normalization, and metadata storage alongside vectors for filtering.

questions.question: How do you index 100M vectors for sub-100ms search?
questions.strong: HNSW or IVF indexes, sharded across nodes, with quantization (PQ) trading a little recall for a lot of memory; name the trade-off explicitly.

questions.question: How do you measure and tune the recall/latency trade-off?
questions.strong: Recall@k against brute-force ground truth on a representative query set; tune efSearch / nprobe; load-test at production QPS, not on a laptop.

questions.question: The embedding model gets upgraded. How do you reindex 100M vectors without downtime?
questions.strong: Build the new index offline in parallel, dual-serve during cutover, version indexes, and roll back by flipping the version pointer.

questions.question: How do you combine vector search with keyword filters and a final ranking stage?
questions.strong: Pre-filter on metadata or post-filter candidates; hybrid dense plus sparse (BM25) with fusion; a cross-encoder or ranker re-scores the top-k.

questions.question: What do you monitor in production?
questions.strong: Latency, recall probes on a golden query set, embedding drift when the model or data changes, and index freshness lag.

rubric.check: Chunk, embed, index, and serve pipeline with metadata for filtering.
Chunking strategy, normalization, and hybrid dense+sparse signals.
Recall@k vs brute force on a golden set; embedding drift detection.
p99 100ms via ANN tuning, sharding, and quantization trade-offs.
Latency, recall probes, freshness lag, and index health.
Click/impression feedback into re-ranking; reindex policy as data grows.
